description: Hi, I'm Ashwin Tewari, a B.Tech student with a passion for technology and problem-solving. I'm looking to collaborate with creative thinkers and developers who are interested in building impactful solutions. Whether you are a coder, designer, or just enthusiastic about space, I'd love to have you on my team!
summary:
Eyes on Mars (incorporating the MARSWALK Mission Portal) is an interactive planetary exploration and mission-planning web application built to prepare future human explorers for safe, science-driven Marswalks.   

What We Developed:
We built a unified browser platform combining a real-time 3D Mars globe (powered by Three.js with IAU planetary rotation and Keplerian orbital mechanics), a multi-layer Leaflet planetary GIS, a five-stop Canvas rover route demo, and a life-support survival simulator. The GIS integrates six NASA and USGS datasets—including MOLA elevation, THEMIS night-time infrared, MRO CTX imagery, Tanaka et al. (2014) geologic units, SHARAD/MARSIS/Phoenix ice evidence, and NASA MMGIS rover traverses—paired with an automated 12-hour data refresh pipeline and a live NASA Image Library search.   

How It Addresses the Challenge & Why It Matters:
Mars data is scattered across separate archives, often separating terrain hazards from scientific targets and blurring measured observations with simulated models. Eyes on Mars bridges that gap by uniting orbital context, localized hazard/resource layers, and a six-criterion Landing-Site Screening Index in one screen. Crucially, every layer displays its instrument, processing method, and uncertainty—strictly separating measured NASA science from clearly labelled simulation parameters so explorers can plan traverses with scientific confidence.
details:
What It Does & How It Works

Eyes on Mars (incorporating the MARSWALK Mission Portal) is an interactive planetary exploration and mission-planning web application designed to synthesize orbital and surface Mars datasets into a single operational workspace. It guides users through a structured mission-planning workflow—from global orbital context down to localized surface traverse and survival analysis:

  1. Interactive 3D Mars Globe & Timeline: Renders a real-time 3D globe of Mars modeling its true 24-hour, 37-minute, 22.66-second sidereal rotation and real-time subsolar illumination using the IAU planetary orientation model. Users can scrub a 2001–2028 mission timeline to inspect 18 surface and orbital spacecraft, tracking live orbital speed and altitude calculated via the Keplerian vis-viva equation.
    • Elevation: 463 m/px Mars Global Surveyor MOLA colour-shaded relief via JPL Mars Trek WMTS.
    • Thermal Inertia Proxy: 100 m/px Mars Odyssey THEMIS night-time infrared mosaics.
    • Morphology & Geology: 5 m/px MRO CTX imagery overlaid with live USGS Tanaka et al. (2014) geologic polygons.
    • Subsurface Ice Evidence: Viking MDIM 2.1 context mosaic paired with citable in-situ detections (2008 Phoenix lander) and orbital radar studies (MRO SHARAD, Mars Express MARSIS).
    • Landing Zones: Verified USGS landing-site feature records and curated mission coordinates.
    • Rover Traverses: Live historical traverse paths for Perseverance and Curiosity pulled from NASA MMGIS feeds.
  2. Landing-Site Screening Index: Evaluates candidate exploration regions across six weighted engineering criteria (Terrain Safety, Surface Hazards, Water Resource Evidence, Thermal Conditions, Communications, and Solar Availability), explicitly flagging MISSING inputs and low-confidence scores rather than fabricating values.
  3. Interactive Rover Route Demo & Colony Survival Simulator: Allows users to drive a five-stop science route on an HTML5 Canvas interface and stress-test outpost life-support margins (oxygen, water, food, energy, habitat integrity, and crew morale) against simulated regional dust storms that cut solar output by 70%.
  4. NASA Data Hub & Automated Sync: Queries the NASA Image and Video Library API in real time and runs an automated 12-hour data refresh pipeline to keep external imagery and layers current while maintaining a transparent Data Provenance Register.

Benefits & Intended Impact

  • Eliminates Data Fragmentation: Instead of cross-referencing separate portals for topography, mineralogy, thermal behavior, and rover tracks, mission planners and researchers can cross-correlate layers in one unified interface.
  • Scientific Transparency & Trust: By attaching a live Scientific Evidence drawer to every map layer—documenting the instrument, spatial resolution, coordinate system, processing method, and uncertainty—the platform prevents users from mistaking visual proxies or game simulations for calibrated measurements.
  • Accessible Education & Early Mission Planning: Built as a lightweight browser tool with zero installation overhead, it serves both students/educators exploring Martian science and early mission planners evaluating candidate EVA ("Marswalk") zones.

Tools, Languages & Software Stack

  • Frontend & Visualization: HTML5, CSS3, Vanilla JavaScript (ES6+), Three.js (r128) for WebGL 3D planetary rendering and orbital mechanics, Leaflet (1.9.4) for 2D equirectangular planetary GIS, HTML5 Canvas, and custom WebAssembly (WASM) acceleration for the secondary 2D planetary globe renderer.
  • APIs & Geospatial Data Services: NASA/JPL Mars Trek WMTS tile services, NASA Image and Video Library REST API (images-api.nasa.gov), USGS Astrogeology ArcGIS REST FeatureServer (Tanaka et al. 2014), and NASA JPL MMGIS rover traverse feeds.
  • Deployment & Automation: Hosted on Render (eyes-on-mars.onrender.com) with an automated 12-hour refresh pipeline for NASA catalog and layer synchronization.

What Makes It Creative

  • Strict "Measured vs. Simulated" Provenance Architecture: Most mission simulators blend real planetary maps with fictional survival metrics without distinction. Eyes on Mars introduces an auditable Data Provenance Register directly in the UI, enforcing a clear boundary between measured orbital observations, literature-derived findings, and simulated mission parameters.
  • "Mars-First" Presentation Mode: Launches directly into an unobstructed, real-time illuminated 3D globe before revealing analytical drawers, letting planetary geometry and orbital motion lead the user experience.
  • Resilient Graceful Degradation: If external NASA WMTS tile servers or ArcGIS endpoints are unreachable due to network restrictions, the app detects tile/feed failures in real time, notifies the user transparently, and seamlessly falls back to embedded global textures and curated records without inventing data.

Key Factors Considered by Our Team

  • Astronaut Safety & Mobility Constraints: When designing the Landing-Site Screening Index and EVA route concepts, we prioritized terrain slope/access risk, thermal extremes, subsurface water-ice accessibility for In-Situ Resource Utilization (ISRU), and dust-storm power degradation.
  • Epistemic Honesty (No Hallucinated Data): We deliberately avoided interpolating or guessing missing site-scale hazard data (such as unmapped boulder fields or local subsurface purity), explicitly labeling incomplete criteria as MISSING and flagging low-confidence scores when fewer than four criteria have verified data.
  • API Reliability & Deprecation: Recognizing that legacy endpoints like the old Mars Rover Photos API are archived, we engineered the Data Hub around the active NASA Image and Video Library API and built automated fallback handling for external geospatial services.
